articles.title: Before Lowell: The Patent System’s Early Rejection of Moral Judgment
articles.content:
美国专利制度的一个根本原则是政府不得基于道德标准拒绝授予专利。我在为另一研究项目阅读大量旧文件时，偶然发现了1812年总检察长威廉·平克尼致国务卿詹姆斯·门罗的备忘录，这份备忘录明确指出政府不能拒绝向被认为道德品行不佳的个人授予专利。詹姆斯·麦克唐纳申请了砖块制造机的专利，当时负责专利事务的国务院似乎因麦克唐纳的行为问题而试图拒绝。平克尼第二天即回复："尽管拒绝授予专利可能是可取的，且申请人的道德行为似乎有问题，但国务院没有权力拒绝发放专利"，只要满足了法定誓言、说明书和模型的要求。专利局170（1812）。十天后，麦克唐纳的专利得以颁发。

根据我的调查，这是美国官员首次明确表示政府无权基于道德理由拒绝授予专利。这份备忘录之所以有趣，部分原因在于其时间背景。它早于詹姆斯·斯托里法官在《洛厄尔诉刘易斯案》（15 F. Cas. 1018, C.C.D. Mass. 1817, No. 8,568）中的著名陈述五年，而该判决被认为是道德实用性原则的源头。见Margo A. Bagley，《专利先行，后续问题：专利法中的道德与生物技术》，45 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 469（2003）（将斯托里视为该原则的首次阐述者）。我发现最后一次引用总检察长备忘录中道德方面内容的文献是威廉·C·罗宾逊1890年的论著："专利不能基于道德理由被拒绝，见1812年总检察长意见，1 Op. At. Gen. 170"。威廉·C·罗宾逊，《有用发明专利法》§ 583 n.2, at 206（1890）。

需要明确的是，道德问题可以区分。洛厄尔案涉及的是发明本身。斯托里法官将法律中的"有用"一词解释为排除"有害于社会福祉、政策或道德的发明"，并举出了投毒、助长淫乱或促成私人谋杀的发明作为例子。平克尼的备忘录则涉及发明者。当时没有人认为砖块机器不道德；反对的是麦克唐纳的行为。尽管如此，我认为这两者属于同一范畴。两者都反映了早期对在授予专利阶段进行道德判断的犹豫。平克尼明确表示国务院没有任何裁量权，将专利的效力问题留给法院。斯托里则将道德语言限定为一种狭窄的标准，同时拒绝更广泛的实用性测试，称"价值不大的发明将默默地陷入蔑视和忽视"。见Juicy Whip, Inc. v. Orange Bang, Inc., 185 F.3d 1364（联邦巡回上诉法院1999）。
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

A fundamental aspect of the U.S. patent system is its lack of moral judgment.

I am doing research for a separate project that involves reading a large number of old documents. Today I came across an interesting 1812 memo from Attorney General William Pinkney to the Secretary of State (James Monroe) concluding that the government could not refuse a patent to a man it considered a moral bad actor. James McDonald had applied for a patent on a brick-making machine, and the Department of State (which then housed the Patent Office) apparently wanted to say no because of McDonald's conduct. Pinkney answered the next day, in two sentences: "however desirable it may be to refuse the patent, and exceptionable as the conduct of the applicant would seem to be upon moral grounds, the Department of State has no discretion to decline to issue the patent as applied for," so long as the statutory oath, specification, and model requirements were satisfied. Patents for Inventions, 1 Op. Att'y Gen. 170 (1812). Ten days later, McDonald's patent issued.

So far as I have found, this is the earliest statement by an American official that the government has no power to withhold a patent on moral grounds. One reason it is interesting is its timing. It came five years before Justice Story's famous charge in Lowell v. Lewis, 15 F. Cas. 1018 (C.C.D. Mass. 1817) (No. 8,568), the decision that serves as the origin of the moral utility doctrine. See Margo A. Bagley, Patent First, Ask Questions Later: Morality and Biotechnology in Patent Law, 45 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 469 (2003) (crediting Story with the doctrine's first articulation). The last citation I found recognizing the moral aspect of the AG's memo is in Robinson's 1890 treatise: "That a patent cannot be withheld on moral grounds, see Opinion Atty. Gen. (1812), 1 Op. At. Gen. 170." 2 William C. Robinson, The Law of Patents for Useful Inventions § 583 n.2, at 206 (1890).

To be clear, the moral questions can be distinguished. Lowell is about the invention. Story read the statutory word "useful" to exclude inventions "injurious to the well-being, good policy, or sound morals of society," and his examples were an invention to poison people, promote debauchery, or facilitate private assassination. Pinkney's memo is about the inventor. Nobody thought a brick machine was immoral; the objection was to McDonald's conduct. Still, I see the two in the same vein. Both reflect an early reluctance to make the grant stage a forum for moral judgment. Pinkney said the Department had no discretion at all and left the patent's efficacy to the courts. Story used his morality language as a narrow floor while rejecting a broader utility test, stating that an invention of little value "will silently sink into contempt and disregard." See also Juicy Whip, Inc. v. Orange Bang, Inc., 185 F.3d 1364 (Fed. Cir. 1999).

To continue reading, become a Patently-O member. Already a member? Simply log in to access the full post.

articles.title: RCEs Are Rising Again: But Applicant Behavior Isn’t the Main Cause
articles.content:
密苏里大学法学教授丹尼斯·克劳奇（Dennis Crouch）撰文指出，美国专利商标局（USPTO）的继续审查请求（RCE）申请数量正在攀升。根据最新数据，截至2026年8月的12个月内，申请人在已公开的实用新型专利申请中提交了近15万份RCE，较前12个月增长13%，这一增长趋势逆转了过去五年的下滑势头。

克劳奇分析称，RCE申请量的增幅主要并非源于申请人最终回复后行为的变化。RCE的选择通常出现在最终驳回通知后，而关键变化在于USPTO近期发出了更多的最终驳回通知——这解释了大部分申请量的增长。此外，2024年12月终止的免费最终审查考虑试点计划（AFCP 2.0）也可能起到了一定作用。原本通过AFCP提交修正的申请人现在直接选择RCE。

至于2025年的收费规则变更，似乎并未显著减缓RCE的增长势头。费用调整将首次RCE费用提高了10%至1500美元，第二次及后续RCE费用提高了43%至2860美元。然而，无论是首次还是后续RCE的申请率均出现了上升。

USPTO最终驳回通知的发出量增加也是一个值得关注的现象，过去一年中该比例达到55%，较之前的50%有所提升。部分原因在于审查重点从续展申请转向了原始申请。克劳奇在此前的文章中指出，USPTO在2022年开始将续展申请提前排入审查队列，并在2025年将其推迟。而原始申请相较于续展申请更容易收到最终驳回通知。不过，这一变化仅能解释部分原因，剩余部分的解释尚不明确。
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

Requests for continued examination are climbing again. Applicants filed nearly 150k RCEs in published utility applications over the 12 months ending August 2026, up 13% from the prior 12 months. That reverses a five-year slide as seen in the chart below.

But, as I explain below, most of the increase is not a change in after-final applicant behavior. The choice to file an RCE arises at a final rejection, and the key change is that the USPTO has been mailing more final rejections – that accounts for most of the increase.  But, we also have the end of the free After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP 2.0) in December 2024. At least some of the Applicants who once tried an AFCP amendment now go straight to an RCE.

It does not appear that the 2025 fee rule slowed things down significantly.  The fee change raised the first RCE fee 10% to $1,500 and second and later RCEs 43% to $2,860.  But the RCE filing rate is up for both first RCEs and subsequent RCEs.

That leaves the question of why the Office is mailing more final rejections: 55 per 100 disposals over the past year, up from 50.  Some of that rise is due to the shift from examining continuations to examining original applications. As I explained in my September 7 post, the Office pulled continuations forward in the examination queue beginning in 2022 and pushed them back in 2025, and original applications are more likely to receive final rejections compared with continuations. But this only explains part of the recent rise (and I don’t have a further explanation).

articles.title: The Federal Circuit Expands Its Jurisdiction Yet Again
articles.content:
Professor Paul Gugliuzza (UTexas) argues in this guest post that the Federal Circuit got the jurisdictional question in Insulet v. EOFlow wrong. He has filed an amicus brief supporting Insulet’s pending petition for rehearing en banc, and makes his case below. — Dennis
Guest post by Professor Paul R. Gugliuzza
Since Congress created the Federal Circuit in 1982, the court has repeatedly expanded the class of cases that, in its view, “arise under” patent law and so fall within its exclusive jurisdiction. The court’s recent decision in Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow Co. is another example. Insulet is a trade secret case. Yet the Federal Circuit held that the case arose under patent law based on its prediction about the outcome of a hypothetical future patent infringement dispute.
The court’s decision overlooks a fundamental principle of the law of federal jurisdiction: namely, that the “arising under” analysis looks solely at the plaintiff’s well-pleaded complaint, not to issues that may (or may not) arise in future litigation.
Some background. In Insulet, the district court entered a $60 million judgment for Insulet on a jury verdict of trade secret misappropriation. Insulet’s original complaint had asserted patent claims, too, but those claims were bifurcated from the trade secret claims, never adjudicated, and eventually dismissed without prejudice by an amendment to Insulet’s complaint.
EOFlow appealed its trial loss to the Federal Circuit. Insulet contested jurisdiction because its amended complaint contained no patent claims, citing a line of circuit precedent holding that, when all patent claims were dismissed without prejudice, the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction.
The court nevertheless heard EOFlow’s appeal on the merits and reversed the trade secret verdict in Insulet’s favor.
In deciding it had jurisdiction, the Federal Circuit’s reasoning went like this:
That sort of multistep analysis resting on conjecture about what might happen in a yet-to-be-filed case is, under both binding Supreme Court precedent and sound principles of judicial administration, the wrong way to decide jurisdiction.
As I argue in an amicus brief supporting Insulet’s pending petition for rehearing en banc, the correct question is, simply: what claims appear in the operative, well-pleaded complaint? In Insulet, the amended complaint contains no patent claims. So, the Federal Circuit does not have jurisdiction. End of story.
Instead, however, the Federal Circuit panel imagined a new patent infringement complaint that Insulet might file in the future, identified a defense EOFlow might raise, and hypothesized how a court would resolve that defense to conclude that the case currently before it did, in fact, arise under patent law.
The 1L civil procedure chestnut, Louisville & Nashville Railroad v. Mottley, fully resolves the jurisdictional dispute in the Insulet case. Under Mottley‘s “well-pleaded complaint rule,” arising under jurisdiction depends on the claims in the plaintiff’s complaint, not on defenses and not on issues that might arise later.
If there were any doubt, the Supreme Court reiterated just last year, in Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger, that, under the well-pleaded complaint rule, an amendment eliminating claims (such as Insulet’s amendment to remove its patent claims) can “wipe the jurisdictional slate clean.”
Insulet isn’t the first time the Federal Circuit has relied on a hypothetical patent dispute to expand its jurisdiction. For instance, the circuit had long held that it had exclusive jurisdiction over state law malpractice cases against patent lawyers because the cases raised questions about what would have happened in a prior patent case had the lawyer not erred.
In Gunn v. Minton, the Supreme Court rejected that line of Federal Circuit precedent. Indeed, the Federal Circuit has a poor record before the Supreme Court on these sorts of jurisdictional or procedural questions.
In a recent study, Mark Lemley and I reviewed every patent-related case the Supreme Court has decided since the Federal Circuit began operating four decades ago. We found that the conventional wisdom about the Federal Circuit (that the Supreme Court is constantly correcting it on matters of substantive patent law) is overstated. Instead, where the Federal Circuit performs poorly is in patent-related cases raising questions of jurisdiction or procedure. In those cases (sixteen in total), the Supreme Court disagreed with the Federal Circuit fifteen times. Including in Gunn.
Those numbers reflect a recurring problem with the Federal Circuit. Congress created the court to provide uniformity and expertise in patent law, but the court has relied on those goals to expand its own authority (vis-à-vis state courts, district courts, and the regional circuits) while ignoring transsubstantive principles of federal law.
Insulet is another example. Instead of applying the well-pleaded complaint rule and sending that trade secret case to the First Circuit, the panel imagined a hypothetical future patent dispute (that might never actually arise) to keep the case in the Federal Circuit.
The en banc court should correct the panel’s error. As Ryan Vacca has shown, though, the Federal Circuit has used en banc review far less often in recent years than it did earlier in its history.
That development removes one of the few ways to correct mistakes of patent law without Supreme Court intervention. When a regional circuit errs, another circuit can disagree, prompting reconsideration or Supreme Court review. On patent law, the Federal Circuit speaks for the whole country.
Supreme Court review supplies a check, but the Court is hearing fewer patent cases than it did a decade ago.
Insulet gives the Federal Circuit a straightforward opportunity to correct itself, for the correct rule is simple: the court should (like all other federal courts) decide jurisdiction by looking at the operative complaint alone.
Paul R. Gugliuzza is the Thomas W. Gregory Professor of Law at University of Texas at Austin School of Law.

In deciding it had jurisdiction, the Federal Circuit’s reasoning went like this:

  • One of Insulet’s dismissed patent claims had alleged an act of infringement in 2018.
  • Section 286 of the Patent Act prohibits recovery for infringement that occurred more than six years before suit.
  • So, if Insulet were to refile its patent infringement claims today, the court would deny recovery for the 2018 act of infringement.
  • Consequently, the dismissal of Insulet’s patent claims, though explicitly “without prejudice,” was, in the Federal Circuit’s view, “function[ally]” a dismissal with prejudice, which establishes Federal Circuit jurisdiction over any subsequent appeal.

That sort of multistep analysis resting on conjecture about what might happen in a yet-to-be-filed case is, under both binding Supreme Court precedent and sound principles of judicial administration, the wrong way to decide jurisdiction.

As I argue in an amicus brief supporting Insulet’s pending petition for rehearing en banc, the correct question is, simply: what claims appear in the operative, well-pleaded complaint? The 1L civil procedure chestnut, Louisville & Nashville Railroad v. Mottley, fully resolves the jurisdictional dispute in the Insulet case. If there were any doubt, the Supreme Court reiterated just last year, in Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger, that, under the well-pleaded complaint rule, an amendment eliminating claims (such as Insulet’s amendment to remove its patent claims) can “wipe the jurisdictional slate clean.”

For instance, the circuit had long held that it had exclusive jurisdiction over state law malpractice cases against patent lawyers because the cases raised questions about what would have happened in a prior patent case had the lawyer not erred.

In Gunn v. Minton, the Supreme Court rejected that line of Federal Circuit precedent. Indeed, the Federal Circuit has a poor record before the Supreme Court on these sorts of jurisdictional or procedural questions.

In a recent study, Mark Lemley and I reviewed every patent-related case the Supreme Court has decided since the Federal Circuit began operating four decades ago. We found that the conventional wisdom about the Federal Circuit (that the Supreme Court is constantly correcting it on matters of substantive patent law) is overstated. Instead, where the Federal Circuit performs poorly is in patent-related cases raising questions of jurisdiction or procedure. In those cases (sixteen in total), the Supreme Court disagreed with the Federal Circuit fifteen times. Including in Gunn.

Those numbers reflect a recurring problem with the Federal Circuit. Congress created the court to provide uniformity and expertise in patent law, but the court has relied on those goals to expand its own authority (vis-à-vis state courts, district courts, and the regional circuits) while ignoring transsubstantive principles of federal law.

Insulet is another example. Instead of applying the well-pleaded complaint rule and sending that trade secret case to the First Circuit, the panel imagined a hypothetical future patent dispute (that might never actually arise) to keep the case in the Federal Circuit.

That development removes one of the few ways to correct mistakes of patent law without Supreme Court intervention. When a regional circuit errs, another circuit can disagree, prompting reconsideration or Supreme Court review. On patent law, the Federal Circuit speaks for the whole country.

Supreme Court review supplies a check, but the Court is hearing fewer patent cases than it did a decade ago.

Insulet gives the Federal Circuit a straightforward opportunity to correct itself, for the correct rule is simple: the court should (like all other federal courts) decide jurisdiction by looking at the operative complaint alone.

Paul R. Gugliuzza is the Thomas W. Gregory Professor of Law at University of Texas at Austin School of Law.
